formal_evidence.equation_description: Equation (1) separates own-school exposure from distance-band treatment density and total density, with school and individual disturbances. This is an experimental reduced-form exposure specification; its regression form alone does not establish structural-econometric or potential-outcome membership.
formal_evidence.location: Printed pp. 175–177; PDF pp. 17–19; equation (1)
formal_evidence.paraphrase: Outcomes depend on first- and second-year school assignment, covariates, nearby pupils in assigned treatment schools, and all nearby pupils. Conditional on total density, random school assignment supplies exogenous exposure variation. School assignment coefficients combine direct and within-school external effects.

formal_evidence.equation_description: The indicator rule D1ij = 1(S(Xijt,eijt) + epsilonijt > Ct) connects observed take-up to gains, unobservables and household costs. Equation (2) decomposes an untreated-group outcome contrast into exposure effects and conditional unobservable differences. Equal costs would remove the latter through randomization; unequal costs require monotonicity of S in health-related unobservables and cross-year dependence. Equation (3) then adds take-up and its interaction with assignment. This integrated behavioral-selection argument supports structural_econometrics membership, although not a fully estimated demand model.
formal_evidence.location: Printed pp. 178, 180–182; PDF pp. 20, 22–24; selection rule and equations (2)–(3)
formal_evidence.paraphrase: A substantive household participation mechanism assumes treatment is obtained when its net gain exceeds a cost threshold. formal_evidence.equation_description: These are explicit restrictions on mechanisms and excluded pathways, rather than graphical intervention assignments. formal_evidence.paraphrase: Assignment cannot instrument individual drug receipt without accounting for spillovers because assignment affects untreated pupils. A separate infection-to-attendance IV analysis imposes the restriction that program attendance gains operate through measured infection; the authors discuss why that restriction may fail. They also acknowledge that optimal subsidies across coverage levels require a fuller behavioral and epidemiological model.
